To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CCM2 interacts with CCM1 via the PTB domain of CCM1, and that CCM2 and CCM1 form a ternary complex with MEKK3.
KRIT1 interacts with malcavernin via its PTB domain.
CCM1 interacts with CCM2, a protein that is mutated in CCM patients, and that the CCM2 mutation abrogates this interaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular pathogenesis of a rare, but devastating, vascular disorder.
the molecular mechanisms of the pathogenesis of CCMs.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that underlie the development of CCM.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CCM proteins form an important complex in cell signaling and that the loss of the CCM1-CCM2 interaction in familial CCM2 mutations may play a key role in pathogenesis.
the CCM2 mutation abrogates CCM1/ICAP1 and CCM1/MEKK3 interactions, and that the loss of these interactions may contribute to the pathogenesis of cerebral cavernous malformation disease.
the CCM2 mutation is not a mutation of CCM2, but rather a mutation that disrupts the CCM1-CCM2 interaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CCM2 and CCM1 form a complex and this complex interacts with MEKK3.
CCM1/ICAP1, CCM1/OSM and CCM1/MEKK3 complexes represent three distinct functional modules that regulate cell adhesion, osmoregulation, and stress signaling, respectively.
the CCM complex, which includes the CCM1, CCM2 and beta1 integrins, is an important signaling complex for the control of cell adhesion, migration and proliferation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CCM proteins may act as scaffolds for signaling complexes that regulate cell adhesion and cell signaling.
the PTB domain of CCM1 interacts with the PTB domain in CCM2 and that this interaction is important for the proper subcellular localization and function of CCM1.
the CCM proteins are involved in a signaling module that may be important for the pathogenesis of CCMs.
